name: The Dig Tree

location.address: Dig Tree Reserve, Nappa Merrie Station, Cooper Creek, Shire of Bulloo, Queensland
location.neighbourhood: Cooper Creek, far south-west Queensland near the South Australian border

access: Publicly accessible: a fenced 4,470 sqm memorial reserve declared by the Queensland Government in 1964, held in trust for the public by the Royal Historical Society of Queensland, physically inside the Nappa Merrie pastoral property but run as a visitor site with interpretive signage, boardwalk and wheelchair access. A conservation/site-management fee (reported around AU$11) is payable at the gate or by QR code. Reached via unsealed Adventure Way roads: about 44km from Innamincka, SA, or 377km from Thargomindah, QLD; caravan-accessible in good weather, can be cut off after rain.
transport: No public transport; self-drive only, on outback dirt roads. Nearest fuel/services at Innamincka, SA (~44km) or Thargomindah, QLD (~377km).
verify_notes: Coordinates match Wikipedia's own infobox figure almost exactly (-27.6237, 141.0758 vs brief's -27.62285805, 141.07527161), so this is a tree-level pin, not a district guess. One of two Coolibahs (Eucalyptus coolabah, listed synonym E. microtheca) on Cooper Creek's north bank blazed by William Brahe's party on 21 April 1861 while Burke, Wills, Gray and King pushed north to the Gulf; Brahe carved 'DIG' pointing to a buried supply cache after his party was forced to abandon the depot camp (Camp LXV) -- Burke and Wills died nearby within months, only King survived. Queensland Heritage Register listed 28 Feb 2003 (id 601073); the reserve itself was gazetted by the Queensland Government on 2 July 1964, predating the heritage listing. Age given as 'reputed 200 to 250 years old' by multiple independent tourism sources, consistent with a mature coolibah of this size; no register girth figure found in this pass, girth_cm left null rather than guessed. Alive and current: the reserve was refurbished in 2020 (interpretive centre, wifi, QR-code fee payment per thedigtree.com.au, the site's own operator), which is recent, credible evidence of active management and continued life; no reports found of the tree having died or fallen. Single-tree-destination test: clearly passes -- this is one of the most famous named trees in Australian history (the Burke and Wills expedition is a national story), heritage-listed, with its own dedicated visitor site and a purpose-built reserve; people travel specifically to Cooper Creek to see it.
